keySentence: Family and integrity matter more than wealth or status.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: The March family faced many years of not having enough money for the things they needed and wanted. But they always had each other and they always treated each other with honesty and genuine kindness. When their father came home from the war they felt richer than any wealthy family they had ever known. When Beth died they grieved together and held each other and did not pretend the pain was not real. When Jo finally found her way as a writer they all celebrated as if her success belonged to all of them. The things that mattered most in their family could not be bought with any amount of money at all. Family and integrity matter more than wealth or status.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: Looking back at Little Women as a whole, the March family's story is primarily a story about values rather than achievements. The girls grow up, pursue their various paths, fall in love, and face significant losses along the way. But the novel's emotional center is always the family itself — the particular quality of love and honesty that the Marches share. When Beth dies, the sisters do not pretend to cope better than they actually do — they grieve authentically and completely. When Jo finally succeeds as a writer, the success is meaningful not primarily as a career achievement but as a family victory. When Meg creates her modest home it is valuable not for its material comfort but for the character of the life lived inside it. Alcott proposes that a life organized around family and integrity — however modest its external circumstances — is a life well lived. Family and integrity matter more than wealth or status.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: The conclusion of Little Women makes a claim that is simple to state and genuinely difficult to live by consistently. Alcott argues, through the accumulated weight of four sisters' stories across two volumes, that external measures of success are secondary. Wealth, social status, beauty, marriage to the right person — none of these, she suggests, are reliable indicators of a life well lived. What indicates a well-lived life is the quality of the relationships it contains and the integrity of the choices that shaped it. This is not a new moral argument — it has been made in various forms across many centuries of ethical thinking. What is distinctive about Little Women is the completeness and honesty with which Alcott tests this argument against reality. She does not pretend that poverty is comfortable or that integrity always produces happiness or that good people are never hurt. She simply shows, through patient and sympathetic observation, that the things which last and which matter are not the ones that money buys. Family and integrity matter more than wealth or status.
